nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer, novelist and editor writing in English
literary_identity: American short-story writer and collagist, the most inventive practitioner of American postmodern fiction, whose hundred-odd stories in The New Yorker remade the short story as a structure of jokes, quotations and interruptions
biography: Donald Barthelme Jr. was born in Philadelphia on 7 April 1931, the son of an architect, and grew up in Houston, Texas, where his father taught at the University of Houston. He studied journalism there, wrote for the Houston Post, founded and edited the literary magazine Forum, was drafted into the army in 1953 and served in Korea as editor of an army newspaper, and in 1961 became director of the Contemporary Arts Museum in Houston, the year he published his first story. He was managing editor of Location and a co-founder of Fiction, and from 1963 The New Yorker published more than a hundred of his stories. Come Back, Dr. Caligari (1964) collected the first of them; Snow White (1967), first serialised in The New Yorker, was his first novel, followed by Unspeakable Practices, Unnatural Acts (1968), City Life (1970), the children's book The Slightly Irregular Fire Engine (1971, National Book Award 1972), Sadness (1972), Guilty Pleasures (1974), The Dead Father (1975), Amateurs (1976), Great Days (1979), Sixty Stories (1981), Overnight to Many Distant Cities (1983), Paradise (1986), Forty Stories (1987) and The King (1990, posthumous). He taught at Boston University, the University at Buffalo and the City College of New York, where he was distinguished visiting professor in 1974-75, and died of throat cancer in Houston on 23 July 1989.
literary_profile: Stories: Come Back, Dr. Caligari (1964), Unspeakable Practices, Unnatural Acts (1968), City Life (1970), Sadness (1972), Amateurs (1976), Great Days (1979), Sixty Stories (1981), Overnight to Many Distant Cities (1983), Forty Stories (1987), Flying to America (2008) and Collected Stories (2021). Novels: Snow White (1967), The Dead Father (1975), Paradise (1986) and The King (1990). Non-fiction and satire: Guilty Pleasures (1974), The Teachings of Don B. (1992) and Not-Knowing (1997). Children's book: The Slightly Irregular Fire Engine (1971).
stylistic_characteristics: Stories without plot in the traditional sense, built by accumulation and juxtaposition; the non-sequitur as a structural device; parody of found forms - the questionnaire, the catalogue, the academic essay, the newspaper column, the interview; dialogue of great flatness and precision; typographic and visual play; a deadpan narrator who reports the absurd as though it were ordinary.
intellectual_concerns: The making of art and the reception of the artwork by a public that wants it explained; the arbitrariness of the signs and objects among which Americans live; marriage, divorce and desire conducted in a language of cliché; the city as a grid and as a joke; death, and the difficulty of saying anything true about it; the exhaustion of inherited literary forms and the freedom that exhaustion offers.
historical_significance: Barthelme is the representative American postmodernist and the writer through whom the American short story after 1965 is usually periodised; his stories are standard anthology and workshop texts, 'The Balloon' and 'The School' are among the most widely reprinted American short stories of the postwar decades, and his influence is acknowledged by writers as different as George Saunders, David Foster Wallace and Lydia Davis. The Library of America collected his stories in 2021, the first such volume for a postwar American experimental short-story writer.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Barthelme and on his bibliography, read directly, with the first periodical printings of the two Norton selections taken from The New Yorker's own archive and from the bibliography's tables; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records the two Norton selections - 'The Balloon' (The New Yorker, 16 April 1966; collected 1968) and 'The School' (The New Yorker, 17 June 1974; collected 1976) - so the novels, the other hundred stories and the non-fiction have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: American poet whose posthumous Ariel (1965) and The Collected Poems (1981) made her the central confessional poet of the postwar period and the most discussed woman poet of the twentieth century
biography: Sylvia Plath was born in the Jamaica Plain district of Boston on 27 October 1932, the daughter of Otto Plath, a German-born professor of biology at Boston University, and Aurelia Schober Plath, a teacher of Austrian descent. Her father died in November 1940, when she was eight, and the grief and anger of that loss became the matter of her best-known poem nineteen years later. She grew up in Wellesley, wrote and published precociously, won a scholarship to Smith College, and in 1953, after a month in New York as a guest editor at Mademoiselle, suffered the first of the breakdowns and suicide attempts that The Bell Jar (1963) describes. She returned to Smith, graduated summa cum laude in 1955, and took a Fulbright to Newnham College, Cambridge, where she met the poet Ted Hughes; they married in June 1956. After two years teaching at Smith she and Hughes moved back to England, and in 1960, after the birth of their daughter Frieda, Heinemann published The Colossus and Other Poems, the only collection of her poetry to appear in her lifetime. In 1961 they settled at Court Green in North Tawton, Devon, where their son Nicholas was born; in the autumn of 1962, after Hughes's affair with Assia Wevill, the marriage broke up and Plath moved with the children to a flat in Fitzroy Road, London. In the last five months of her life she wrote at extraordinary speed - the poems of October and November 1962, including 'Daddy', 'Lady Lazarus', 'Ariel' and 'The Applicant', and the winter poems 'Child' and 'Words' - and in January 1963 published The Bell Jar under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas. She died by suicide in London on 11 February 1963, aged thirty, and is buried at Heptonstall in West Yorkshire. Ariel appeared in 1965 in a text arranged by Hughes, who reordered the manuscript and added poems; Ariel: The Restored Edition (2004) printed her own selection and sequence for the first time. The Collected Poems (1981), also edited by Hughes, won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1982, the first awarded posthumously to a poet.
literary_profile: Poetry: The Colossus and Other Poems (1960), Ariel (1965), Uncollected Poems (1965), Crossing the Water (1971), Winter Trees (1971), The Collected Poems (1981, Pulitzer Prize 1982), Selected Poems (1985) and Ariel: The Restored Edition (2004). Novel: The Bell Jar (1963, as Victoria Lucas). Prose and letters: Letters Home (1975), Johnny Panic and the Bible of Dreams (1977), The Journals of Sylvia Plath (1982), The Unabridged Journals (2000) and The Letters of Sylvia Plath (2 vols, 2017-2018). Children's books: The Bed Book (1976) and The It-Doesn't-Matter Suit (1996).
stylistic_characteristics: Short stanzas, usually tercets, quintains or loose quatrains, with lines that run over the stanza break and a rhyme that is heard in the vowel rather than at the line end; a diction that moves without warning between the nursery and the clinic, the lyric and the obscene; a first person that is at once exhibitionistic and defensive; repetition and refrain used as a formal device, as in 'Daddy' and 'Lady Lazarus'; the homeliest domestic object - a watch, a shoe, a telephone, a paperweight - made to carry the whole weight of the poem.
intellectual_concerns: The father as the dead origin of speech; the wish to die and the theatrical refusal to stay dead; motherhood, childbirth and the body as the site of another's life; marriage, betrayal and the humiliation of dependence; the Holocaust and the concentration camp as figures for domestic power; the English and American landscape as an image of the mind; the materials of a woman's art - sewing, cooking, beekeeping, riding, drawing - turned into the machinery of vision.
historical_significance: Plath is the poet through whom confessional poetry and the literature of the 1960s are taught, and 'Daddy', 'Lady Lazarus' and 'Ariel' are among the most anthologised and most argued-over poems of the century. Her posthumous reputation - the Pulitzer of 1982, the biographies, the controversy over the editing of Ariel, the part she plays in feminist criticism from the 1970s onward - has made her a case study in the making of a literary reputation as well as a body of work, and her influence on later women poets in English is acknowledged almost everywhere it is discussed.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Sylvia Plath, on Ariel and on The Colossus and Other Poems, which agree with the contents list of The Collected Poems and with the dates of composition established from the manuscripts at Smith College and printed in the appendix to Ariel: The Restored Edition; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records the eight Norton selections - 'Morning Song', 'Lady Lazarus', 'Ariel', 'Daddy', 'Words', 'Blackberrying', 'The Applicant' and 'Child' - so the other poems, the novel, the stories, the letters and the journals have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.
